'''''Hesperocyparis arizonica''''', the '''Arizona cypress''', is a [[species]] of [[conifer]] in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]], [[native species|native]] to the southwestern United States and Mexico. Populations may be scattered rather than in large, dense stands.

==Description==
[[File:Hesperocyparis arizonica - CK Kelly 01.jpg|thumb|left|''Hesperocyparis arizonica'' tree in [[Chiricahua National Monument]], Arizona]]
''Hesperocyparis arizonica'' is a [[conifer]]ous tree with a [[cone|conic]] to ovoid-conic crown. It grows to heights of {{cvt|10–25|m|ft|abbr=on}}, and its trunk diameter reaches {{cvt|55|cm|in|abbr=on}}. The foliage grows in dense sprays, varying from dull gray-green to bright [[glaucous]] blue-green. The leaves are scale-like, 2–5 mm long, and produced on rounded (not flattened) shoots. The seed [[conifer cone|cones]] are [[globose]] to oblong, 15–33 mm long, with 6 or 8 (rarely 4 or 10) scales, green at first, maturing gray or gray-brown about 20–24 months after pollination. The cones remain closed for many years, only opening after the bearing branch is killed (in a [[wildfire]] or otherwise), allowing the [[seed]]s to colonize the bare ground exposed by the fire. The male cones are 3–5 mm long, and release pollen in February–March.<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|200005413|Cupressus arizonica |first=James E. |last=Eckenwalder |volume=2}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Hesperocyparis arizonica'' was given its first scientific name and described by [[Edward Lee Greene]] in 1882 as ''Cupressus arizonica'', placing it in genus ''[[Cupressus]]''.<ref name="POWO" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Greene |first1=Edward Lee |title=New Western Plants |journal=Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club |date=May 1882 |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=64–65 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/648344 |access-date=27 January 2024 |publisher=Torrey Botanical Club |location=New York}}</ref> This description was soon after disputed by [[Maxwell T. Masters]] who, in 1896, published a journal article where he said it should be considered a subspecies of ''[[Cupressus benthamii]]'' with the [[variety (botany)|variety]] name of ''arizonica''.<ref name="POWO" /> A similar classification reducing it to a subspecies as ''[[Cupressus lusitanica]]'' subsp. ''arizonica'' was posthumously published by [[René Maire]] in 1952.<ref name="POWO" /> There also have been publications that suggested moving it as a species to a different genus such as ''[[Callitropsis nootkatensis|Callitropsis]]'' in 2006 and a new genus, ''Neocupressus'', in 2009.<ref name="POWO" /> 

As of 2024 [[Plants of the World Online]] (POWO), [[World Flora Online]] (WFO), and the USDA [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] PLANTS database (PLANTS) list ''H. arizonica'' as the correct species name.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="WFO" /><ref name="USDA">{{cite usda plants|symbol=HEAR22 |title=Hesperocyparis arizonica |date=13 February 2024}}</ref> This classification was published by Jim A. Bartel in 2009.<ref name="POWO" /> However, ''Cupressus'' continues to be used in professional papers by some scientists.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Michalet |first1=Richard |last2=Carcaillet |first2=Christopher |last3=Delerue |first3=Florian |last4=Domec |first4=Jean-Christophe |last5=Lenoir |first5=Jonathan |title=Assisted migration in a warmer and drier climate: less climate buffering capacity, less facilitation and more fires at temperate latitudes? |journal=Oikos |date=19 December 2023 |volume=2024 |issue=8 |doi=10.1111/oik.10248 |s2cid=266410521 |url=https://nsojournals-onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/oik.10248 |access-date=13 February 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Raddi |first1=Paolo |last2=Della Rocca |first2=Gianni |last3=Danti |first3=Roberto |editor1-last=Stimm |editor1-first=B. |editor2-last=Roloff |editor2-first=A. |editor3-last=Lang |editor3-first=U.M. |editor4-last=Weisgerber |editor4-first=H. |title=Enzyklopädie der Holzgewächse: Handbuch und Atlas der Dendrologie /begründet von Peter Schütt. Andreas Roloff; Horst Weisgerber; Ulla M. Lang; Bernd Stimm |date=8 January 2020 |publisher=Wiley-VCH |location=Weinheim |isbn=978-3-527-32141-4 |language=en |chapter=Cupressus glabra}}</ref>

Other disagreements have been over the validity of various subspecies of ''H. arizonica''. A total of eleven have been validly published. However seven of these are listed as [[synonym (botany)|synonyms]] by  POWO and WFO as of 2024.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="WFO">{{Cite WFO |title=''Hesperocyparis arizonica'' (Greene) Bartel |id=0000912962 |access-date=27 January 2024}}</ref> The remaining four are listed as separate species:
* ''[[Hesperocyparis glabra]]'' formerly ''Cupressus arizonica'' var. ''glabra'' – Smooth Arizona cypress<ref>{{cite POWO |id=60451551-2 |title=''Hesperocyparis glabra'' (Sudw.) Bartel |access-date=27 January 2024}}</ref>
* ''[[Hesperocyparis montana]]'' formerly ''Cupressus arizonica'' var. ''montana'' – San Pedro Mártir cypress<ref>{{cite POWO |id=60451559-2 |title=''Hesperocyparis montana'' (Wiggins) Bartel |access-date=27 January 2024}}</ref>
* ''[[Hesperocyparis nevadensis]]'' formerly ''Cupressus arizonica'' var. ''nevadensis'' – Paiute cypress<ref>{{cite POWO |id=60451560-2 |title=''Hesperocyparis nevadensis'' (Abrams) Bartel |access-date=27 January 2024}}</ref>
* ''[[Hesperocyparis stephensonii]]'' formerly ''Cupressus arizonica'' var. ''stephensonii'' – Cuyamaca cypress<ref>{{cite POWO |id=60451562-2 |title=''Hesperocyparis stephensonii'' (C.B.Wolf) Bartel |access-date=27 January 2024}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Hesperocyparis arizonica'' is found mainly in northern Mexico in the states of [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[Coahuila]], [[Durango]], [[Tamaulipas]], and [[Zacatecas]]. It is also found in small areas of the southwestern United States in the southern parts of [[Arizona]], [[New Mexico]], and [[Texas]]. In the US it is found at {{cvt|1000–1500|m|-3}} elevation, while in Mexico it reaches as high as {{cvt|2200|m|-2}} in some forests.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Earle |first1=Christopher J. |title=''Cupressus arizonica'' (Arizona cypress) description |url=https://www.conifers.org/cu/Cupressus_arizonica.php |website=The Gymnosperm Database |access-date=28 January 2024 |language=en |date=3 March 2023}}</ref><ref name="POWO" /> In the wild, the species is often found in small, scattered populations, not necessarily in large forests. An example occurrence is within the [[Sierra Juárez and San Pedro Mártir pine–oak forests]] of Mexico,{{sfn|National Geographic|2001}} where it is found along with [[Quercus chrysolepis|canyon live oak]] and [[Washingtonia filifera|California fan palm]].

==Uses==
Arizona cypress is widely cultivated as an ornamental tree. Unlike [[Cupressus macrocarpa|Monterey cypress]], it has proved highly resistant to [[cypress canker]],{{original research inline|date=June 2025}} caused by the fungus ''[[Lepteutypa|Seiridium]] cardinale'', and growth is reliable where this disease is prevalent.{{original research inline|date=June 2025}} 

The [[cultivar]] 'Pyramidalis'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Cupressus arizonica'' 'Blue Ice'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/85769/Cupressus-arizonica-Pyramidalis/Details | access-date=15 April 2020}}</ref> has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]] (confirmed 2017).<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 26 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 24 January 2018}}</ref>

==Example of neoendemism and conservation challenges==
The ease of [[hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] of [[western cypress]] species in the [[American southwest]] has fostered a parallel history of [[taxonomy|taxonomic]] disagreements of where genus and species distinctions should apply.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rehfeldt |first1=Gerald E |title=Quantitative analyses of the genetic structure of closely related conifers with disparate distributions and demographics: the ''Cupressus arizonica'' (Cupressaceae) complex |journal=American Journal of Botany |date=1997 |volume=84 |issue=2 |pages=190–200 |doi=10.2307/2446080 |jstor=2446080 |pmid=21712198 |url=https://bsapubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.2307/2446080|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It thus provides a case study of [[neoendemism]] in conifers. Close taxonomic relatedness, in turn, offers both challenges and opportunities if and when [[assisted migration]] is considered as a mode of [[climate adaptation]] to prevent extinctions of endemic cypresses in the American southwest.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Barlow |first1=Connie |title=Climate, Trees, and Legacy: 04 - Lessons of Arizona Cypress |url=https://youtube.com/vW_Zaowal8k |website=youtube |publisher=ghostsofevolution |access-date=14 December 2022 }}{{Dead link|date=December 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>
